title: Religion in Ireland
text:
Over 90% of Irish primary schools are run by a religious patron, most of them Catholic, and the State’s auditor has found that 85% of schools are built on land owned by patrons or trustees. At the same time, fewer people say they’re Catholic at every census, and civil ceremonies are now as common as Catholic weddings.
This project tracks the place of religion in Irish public life using open data, mainly from the Central Statistics Office, the Department of Education and the Charities Regulator. The code behind every figure is on GitHub.

Catholic marriages plummet as civil ceremonies surge


Figure 1. Opposite-sex marriages registered in Ireland by form of ceremony, 2000 to 2024. In 2000, 80% of marriages were Roman Catholic ceremonies and 16% were civil. title: Shankill to Killiney: a bike lane that’s a beach
text: Part of Cycling infrastructure in Dublin. See also the Blackrock DART laneway.

title: Shankill to Killiney: a bike lane that’s a beach
text:
What the map says
Ask Google Maps for cycling directions from Shankill to Killiney and it sends you down to the shore and north along the coast: 2.8 km, nine minutes, most of it shown in dark green and labelled “Separate bike lane”.




Google Maps cycling directions from Shankill to Killiney, 6 November 2026. The green section along the shore is labelled “Separate bike lane”.

title: Shankill to Killiney: a bike lane that’s a beach
text:
What’s actually there
From the Shankill end there’s a short stretch of path. After that, the “bike lane” is the beach below the Shanganagh cliffs and the seafront walls: loose, rounded stones, shingle and rough grass, with no path, surface or markings of any kind. You can’t ride a bike on it, and pushing one is hard work. It isn’t usable with a buggy or a wheelchair either.






Looking north along the shore towards Killiney Hill and Dalkey Island. The whole route is loose shingle.







Large rounded stones below the seafront houses, where the map shows a bike lane.









Stones, grass and ivy-covered walls. There is no path.







Further north, the stones run right up to the walls.








Looking north towards Killiney. Photos taken in early November 2026. A person in the background has been blurred.


The council agrees the shore is difficult. Its own page for the Corbawn Lane beach access, about 500 metres from Shankill DART station, says the strand “is unsuitable for those with disabilities due to the stoney terrain and dangers posed by unstable cliffs” (DLR, Corbawn Lane).

title: Shankill to Killiney: a bike lane that’s a beach
text:
Is anything planned?
I found no council or National Transport Authority plan for a walking or cycling path along this stretch of shore. What I did find:

The Coastal Mobility Route stops well north of here. DLR’s coastal cycleway runs from Booterstown and Blackrock to Sandycove and Dalkey (DLR, Coastal Mobility Interventions). There is no equivalent route from Killiney south to Shankill.
Coastal protection, not access. In 2018 to 2019 DLR rebuilt the Corbawn Lane beach access and put rock armour along about 180 metres of cliff to the north, costing about €928,000 (DLR, December 2018; Afloat). The works protected the cliff and the steps, not a route along the shore.
Irish Rail’s sea defences. Irish Rail’s East Coast Railway Infrastructure Protection Project proposes rock armour and higher sea walls between Merrion Gates and Wicklow, including a section from Dalkey Tunnel to Shanganagh. It consulted the public in autumn 2025 and expects works to run to about 2029. RTÉ reported that “access routes to the public will be maintained and improved in some places”, and that some beaches may get narrower (RTÉ, September 2025). If this goes ahead, it’s the one current project that will reshape this shore, so it’s the moment to ask for a path.
A coastal walk was suggested in 2017, further south, from Bray to Shankill. A councillor proposed referring the idea to a council committee, and another pointed to Woodbrook Golf Club and cliff erosion as obstacles (Bray People, July 2017).

I haven’t found any news coverage of the Google Maps label itself.

title: Shankill to Killiney: a bike lane that’s a beach
text:
Questions for the council

Does DLR consider the shore between Shankill and Killiney DART stations to be part of its cycle network? If not, will it ask Google to remove the “separate bike lane” label?
Are there plans for a walking and cycling path between Shankill and Killiney, along the coast or inland, and is it in the DLR or NTA cycle network plans?
Is DLR talking to Irish Rail about building public access, or a path, into the East Coast Railway Infrastructure Protection Project along this stretch?
Until there’s a path, what’s the recommended cycle route between Shankill and Killiney?

You can also report the label to Google directly: in Google Maps, tap the route and choose Send feedback.

title: Lower Kilmacud Road: the lane that ends at a school gate
text: Part of Cycling infrastructure in Dublin. See also Stillorgan village.

title: Lower Kilmacud Road: the lane that ends at a school gate
text:
The gap
In the words of local councillor Eoin O’Driscoll, the “existing cycle lane currently comes to an end outside Mount Anville Primary School”. From there you’re in traffic, on a road busy with school runs and through traffic heading for the N11.

title: Lower Kilmacud Road: the lane that ends at a school gate
text:
What’s planned
The fix is the DLR Connector, an 8–8.5 km active travel route from Nutgrove to Dún Laoghaire, about 6 km of it new. It’s estimated at about €45 million and funded by the National Transport Authority (NTA). It would carry a continuous cycle track along Lower Kilmacud Road and across the N11.
Public consultation ran from 3 June to 15 July 2025. The council planned to apply for planning permission by the end of 2025. That slipped: in October 2026 the application was expected to go to An Coimisiún Pleanála in the third or fourth quarter of 2026. Construction is pencilled in for 2027 to the end of 2028.

title: Lower Kilmacud Road: the lane that ends at a school gate
Lower Kilmacud Road: the lane that ends at a school gate
text:
Questions for the council

Has the DLR Connector been submitted to An Coimisiún Pleanála? If not, when will it be?
What’s the current timeline for construction on the Lower Kilmacud Road section?
Until then, can anything be done at the end of the existing lane outside Mount Anville Primary, for example a protected transition or a lower speed limit at school times?
What changes were made to the design after the 2025 consultation, particularly track widths and the N11 junction?
Will the route include a permanent counter?

title: Coastal Mobility Route: six years on, still temporary
text: Part of Cycling infrastructure in Dublin. Usage on this route is tracked on the DLR cycle counters page.

title: Coastal Mobility Route: six years on, still temporary
text:
What’s there now
The Coastal Mobility Route (CMR) runs about 4.5 km along the coast road from Blackrock to Sandycove. About 3.6 km of it is a two-way cycle track separated from traffic. It went in during summer 2020 as a temporary Covid measure, built from bollards, paint and plastic kerbs, and that’s still largely what’s on the ground.
It’s one of the busiest cycle routes in the county. The council’s counter at Seapoint averaged 1,053 cyclists a day in the 12 months to September 2026, up 3% on the year before. The counter at People’s Park in Dún Laoghaire averaged about 794 a day.
The temporary layout leaves gaps where the segregation stops and you’re back in traffic, at Newtown Avenue, Crofton Road, Queen’s Road and Sandycove Avenue.

title: Coastal Mobility Route: six years on, still temporary
Coastal Mobility Route: six years on, still temporary
text:
Current status
The consultation page was last updated on 1 December 2025. As of November 2026 we couldn’t find a published construction date, a tender or a contract for the permanent scheme. A short closure of the route in August 2026 was for ground investigation at the Blackrock DART laneway, not for this scheme.

title: The Blackrock DART laneway
text: Part of Cycling infrastructure in Dublin. See also Shankill to Killiney.

title: The Blackrock DART laneway
text:
The problem
Between Blackrock Park and Bath Place, at the entrance to Blackrock DART station, the Coastal Mobility Route squeezes into a single lane between high walls. It’s the only direct link between the park’s paths and the station, and Google Maps sends cycle routes through it.
The lane is about 1.2 metres wide (Part 8 report), and about 90 metres of it has walls on both sides (IrishCycle, January 2026). Two bikes can’t pass each other in it. Nor can a bike and a buggy, or two buggies. Signs tell people on bikes to dismount, so everyone queues at each end and goes through in turns. Local councillor Marie Baker put it plainly: “you end up flattening yourself against the wall if you come up to a cyclist” (IrishCycle, April 2024).




The laneway on Google Maps, from Blackrock Park (top) down to Bath Place and the station (bottom). The pin is at 53°18’12.1”N 6°10’49.4”W, where the park path enters the lane.



View on OpenStreetMap

title: The Blackrock DART laneway
text:
Current status of the laneway
DLR’s Blackrock DART to Park Active Travel Scheme replaces the lane with a new route through part of the garden of Deepwell House next door: 130 metres of two-way cycle track 3 to 3.65 metres wide, a separate 2 metre footpath, grass verges, and a new bridge over the Priory Stream. The old lane will be closed off (DLR Part 8 report; DLR PPN).


April 2024
Plan published


June to August 2024
Public consultation: 321 submissions, about 81% in favour as proposed


October 2024
Councillors approve the scheme


November to December 2025
Compulsory purchase order: no objections


August 2026
Lane closed 24 to 28 August for ground investigation


Not yet scheduled
Construction



Planning. The Part 8 consultation ran from 28 June to 9 August 2024 and drew 321 submissions. Councillors agreed the Chief Executive’s recommendations at their October 2024 meeting (DLR; Citizen Space; Chief Executive’s report).
Land. The council’s compulsory purchase order for part of the Deepwell House garden went to An Coimisiún Pleanála (formerly An Bord Pleanála) on 11 November 2025 and closed with no objections received on 8 December 2025 (case 323857; IrishCycle, January 2026). At the time, Cllr Baker said there was “some paperwork to be completed and then detailed design to take place before work commences.”
Site investigation. The council closed the lane from 24 to 28 August 2026 for ground investigation. Cllr Conor Dowling said: “While the main works will not commence for a few months, this is real progress” (IrishCycle, August 2026).
Construction. As of 7 November 2026 I could find no published start date, construction period or budget. The council’s report treats cost estimates as commercially sensitive.

title: The Blackrock DART laneway
section: How many people cycle here, and how many go around?
text:
How many people cycle here, and how many go around?
The council counted people on the laneway route on three weekdays in November 2022, from 7am to 7pm. Two survey points along the route averaged 406 and 476 cyclists a day and 1,373 and 772 pedestrians a day (Part 8 report, Table 4-3; a third point recorded 68 cyclists).
DLR also runs permanent bicycle counters and publishes the hourly counts as open data. Three are on Rock Road at Booterstown, about a kilometre west of the lane: the cycle track, the bus lane, and a path counter it calls “Rock Road Park”. Another is on the Coastal Mobility Route at Seapoint, about a kilometre and a half east. Here’s what they counted over the same three days and hours.


Figure 1. Average cyclists per weekday, 7am to 7pm, 8 to 10 November 2022. Blue: DLR’s permanent counters on Rock Road and at Seapoint. Orange: the council’s survey of the laneway route. Data: DLR, bicycle counts (CC BY), and the Part 8 report. Code: make_cycling_charts.py. Open full screen.
On those days about 1,670 cyclists a day passed the Rock Road counters and about 900 passed Seapoint, but only 400 to 480 used the laneway route. So the lane carried at most about half as many cyclists as the coastal route at Seapoint. Most people cycling the coast between Booterstown and Seapoint appear to stay on Rock Road and go through Blackrock village rather than take the park and the lane.
That’s consistent with people avoiding the lane, but it doesn’t prove it. Some of the people on these counters are heading to Blackrock village or turning inland, and nobody counts which way each person goes. The council’s own counts are also from just three days. What the numbers do give is a baseline. Once the new path opens, the same counters will show whether people switch from the road to the park route.


Figure 2. Average cyclists per day by month, all days, from DLR’s permanent counters. The Seapoint counter started in September 2020, when the Coastal Mobility Route opened. Days with counter faults (missing hours, or totals of zero or under a quarter of the usual level) are left out, and months with fewer than 10 good days are blank. Data: DLR, bicycle counts and counter locations (CC BY). Code: make_cycling_charts.py. Open full screen.
Cycling on this stretch has held steady since the pandemic peak. In 2025 the Rock Road road counters averaged about 1,130 cyclists a day, the park path about 520, and Seapoint about 1,030, every day of the year.

title: About
text:
Fianaise takes open data about Irish public life and makes it readable: charts and maps, a few sentences on what they show, and the data and code behind each one. The aim is to keep the public informed and to help hold institutions to account, by doing the analysis that journalists and policymakers often don’t have the time to do.
Fianaise is Irish for evidence.
My name is Maedbh King. I grew up in Dublin and spent 10 years in North America, where I did a PhD in Psychology at the University of California, Berkeley and a postdoctoral fellowship at MIT. I moved back to Ireland with my family in summer 2025, and now work in strategy and policy at Trinity College Dublin. Fianaise is independent of my employer and is done in my own time.
If you spot a mistake, please open an issue on GitHub (there is a form for corrections). Corrections are made in the open, and the change history of every page is public on GitHub. If you’d like to see a particular analysis, or have some feedback, please email fianaise@proton.me.
Text and figures are licensed CC BY 4.0: reuse them freely, with credit to Fianaise. Code is MIT licensed. The underlying data belongs to its publishers and keeps their licences (see Data & code).

title: Blackrock village: Living Streets works and the closed contraflow
text: Part of Cycling infrastructure in Dublin. See also the Blackrock DART laneway and the Coastal Mobility Route.

title: Blackrock village: Living Streets works and the closed contraflow
text:
The scheme
In 2020 Blackrock Main Street got a temporary layout with more space for walking and a southbound contraflow cycle lane outside the library. The contraflow links the village to Maretimo Villas and on to the Coastal Mobility Route, so you can ride south through the village without going round the one-way system.
The council’s Living Streets: Blackrock Village scheme makes that layout permanent. Consultation closed on 10 June 2023. Clonmel Enterprises won the contract, and works started in October 2025. It costs about €6.3 million excluding VAT, of which more than €3 million is from the NTA. Substantial completion is expected in the first quarter of 2027.

title: Blackrock village: Living Streets works and the closed contraflow
text:
During the works
A reader comment on IrishCycle on 3 August 2026 said the “contra flow lane has been closed for months”. We haven’t found an official notice of the closure or of a signed diversion, and we’d like the council to confirm.
The council’s latest updates say resurfacing will happen in the New Year (update of 20 October 2026), and there was night work at the Rock Road and Rock Hill junction on 3 November 2026, from 7pm to 11pm.

What’s the signed diversion for people cycling south through the village while it’s closed?
Is the scheme still on track for substantial completion in the first quarter of 2027?
Will the finished contraflow be physically protected from traffic and parking?

title: DLR cycle counters
text:
Part of Cycling infrastructure in Dublin. The Seapoint and People’s Park counters are on the Coastal Mobility Route, and the Rock Road counters are just south of the gap at Merrion Gates. The Blackrock DART laneway page uses both.
Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council (DLR) has permanent automatic counters on its main cycle routes. They count every bike that passes, every hour, and the council publishes the counts as open data. This page turns them into charts. It checks for new data every week and updates itself when there is some.
Data to 30 September 2026, from 16 counters. Counting started in 2010.
* Readings at The Metals jump between about 100 and 900 a day from one month to the next since late 2024, which looks like a counter fault. Treat its numbers with caution.

title: Cycling infrastructure in Dublin
text:
Some of the routes that Google Maps and the councils show as cycle routes are hard or impossible to cycle: a path that turns into a stony beach, or a walled lane too narrow for two bikes to pass. Each one breaks a route that is otherwise good, and pushes people back onto busy roads or off their bikes.
This project documents those gaps, and the routes I cycle regularly, one at a time, with photos taken on the ground, what the map claims, and what the council has said or planned. Each page ends with questions for Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown County Council (DLR). Pages are updated when there’s news.

title: Rock Road: the cycle track that stops at the county boundary
text: Part of Cycling infrastructure in Dublin. Usage here is tracked on the DLR cycle counters page. See also the Coastal Mobility Route.

title: Rock Road: the cycle track that stops at the county boundary
text:
What was built
DLR consulted on extending the Coastal Mobility Route from Blackrock Park to Trimleston Avenue from 6 to 27 April 2022. It got 260 submissions: 59% supported it as proposed and another 21% supported it with changes.
Actavo built it between October 2022 and June 2023: about 400–450 m of two-way cycle track on the seaward side of Rock Road, planned at a minimum of 3 m wide. It was nearly open by July 2023, and it’s a good stretch of track.

title: Rock Road: the cycle track that stops at the county boundary
text:
Where it stops
The track ends at Trimleston Avenue, which is where Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown meets Dublin City. North of there, towards Merrion Gates and Strand Road, is Dublin City Council’s road. Heading north you have to cross over and mix with traffic on Merrion Road. Dublin City’s own plans for this stretch were tied up with the Strand Road cycle route and its court case.
When it consulted in 2022, DLR said feedback about the city side would be passed on to Dublin City Council.

title: Rock Road: the cycle track that stops at the county boundary
text:
How many people use it
The three Rock Road counters at Booterstown averaged about 1,620 cyclists a day between them in the 12 months to September 2026: 630 on the cycle track, 454 in the bus lane and 540 on the park path. Every one of those riders heading for the city reaches the end of the track.

title: Rock Road: the cycle track that stops at the county boundary
text:
Questions for the council

What has DLR heard back from Dublin City Council about continuing the track from Trimleston Avenue to Merrion Gates?
Is there a joint DLR and DCC plan or timeline for that link?
Can the crossing at the end of the track be improved in the meantime, so northbound riders aren’t left on Merrion Road with traffic?
The Rock Road cycle track counter was inbound only until 2026. Does it now count both directions, and from what date?

The contact is DLR’s Active Travel team, cycling@dlrcoco.ie.

title: Stillorgan village: Old Dublin Road still waiting
text: Part of Cycling infrastructure in Dublin. See also Lower Kilmacud Road.

title: Stillorgan village: Old Dublin Road still waiting
text:
The plan
DLR consulted on the Stillorgan Village Area Movement Framework Plan from 28 October to 9 December 2015. It’s being built in phases. Phases 1 and 2, on Lower Kilmacud Road between South Avenue and Kilmacud Crokes, are done.

title: Stillorgan village: Old Dublin Road still waiting
text:
Phase 4A: Old Dublin Road
Phase 4A covers the Old Dublin Road from St Lawrence’s Park to Stillorgan College of Further Education. The council consulted from 21 May to 18 June 2025 and got 125 submissions, and the report was noted in December 2025.
The published plans are for wider footpaths and public realm work. We couldn’t find a cycle track in them.
Construction was due to start in the second quarter of 2026. In January 2026 that moved to the first quarter of 2027.

title: Stillorgan village: Old Dublin Road still waiting
text:
The rest
Phases 3 and 4B, covering Lower Kilmacud Road, The Hill and the rest of the Old Dublin Road, have no published timing.

title: Stillorgan village: Old Dublin Road still waiting
text:
Questions for the council

Does Phase 4A include any cycling provision on the Old Dublin Road? If not, why not?
Is the first quarter of 2027 still the start date for Phase 4A?
When will Phases 3 and 4B be designed and consulted on?
How will the Stillorgan village phases connect to the DLR Connector on Lower Kilmacud Road?

The contact is DLR’s Active Travel team, cycling@dlrcoco.ie.

title: Fianaise
text:
Fianaise is an independent project analysing open data on Irish cultural, religious and civic life. Ireland publishes a great deal of open data, from the Central Statistics Office, government departments and public registers, but most of it sits in spreadsheets that journalists, policymakers and the public rarely have the time to dig through. Fianaise turns that data into charts, maps and short analysis, with the data and code behind every figure, so anyone can check it and use it.
Fianaise is Irish for evidence. You can reach me at fianaise@proton.me.

title: Primary School Survey 2026
text:
Part of Religion in Ireland. See also Schools for who runs Ireland’s primary schools today.
Over 90% of Irish primary schools are denominational, yet recent survey data (June 2026) shows substantial and widespread parental demand for multi-denominational education. The charts and maps below explore that gap, school by school and county by county, with a particular focus on how the preferences of parents differ from those of school staff and boards of management.
The data comes from the Department of Education and Youth’s 2025–2026 Primary School Survey and its results summary report. The results for staff and boards of management are not in the spreadsheet the Department publishes, only in the summary report. The code is on GitHub. The figures are interactive.

title: Primary School Survey 2026
section: The first survey of its kind
text:
The first survey of its kind
The Department described the survey as “the largest of its kind ever undertaken in Ireland” (press release, 4 November 2025).


What the Department set out to do
“Assess parental demand for different types of primary school provision”: ethos, co-education or single-sex, and English- or Irish-medium.


Who was asked

Parents of children in primary school, and of children not yet enrolled
One response per household, validated by Eircode
Separately, school staff and boards of management





4 Nov 2025
Survey opens online


16 Dec 2025
Survey closes: 200,381 valid parent and 32,901 staff and board responses


7 Apr 2026
National parent results published


June 2026
Each school receives its own report. The summary report adds county results for parents and for staff and boards


Oct–Nov 2026
Boards decide whether to act on their results


Staff and board results are published nationally and by county, but not school by school, for privacy reasons.

The survey in numbers


Figure 1. Eligible population, responses received and valid responses, for parents and guardians and for school staff and boards of management. Parental response rates by county ran from 31.5% (Louth) to 63.4% (Meath). Source: results summary report (June 2026). Code: make_charts.py.

title: Primary School Survey 2026
text:
Preference far exceeds current provision


Figure 2. The share of households that prefer a multi-denominational school (all households, results summary report, Table 2a), against the share of pupils and of schools that are multi-denominational today (the Department’s latest school list; see Schools). Code: make_maps.py.


Figure 3. Denominational schools where most parents prefer a multi-denominational ethos (orange), against schools that are already multi-denominational (green). Click the legend to show or hide a group, and hover over or tap a school for its survey results. Code: make_maps.py. Open full screen.

Figure 4. Share preferring a multi-denominational school in each county: parents of children not yet in school (dark orange), parents of children in school (light orange), and school staff and boards of management (dark). Counties are sorted by the staff and board figure. The shaded band is the gap between staff and boards and parents. Source: results summary report, Tables 3, 7 and 8; the denominational-school figures are from sections 3.1.2 (p. 14) and 4.3 (p. 26). Code: make_charts.py.






NoteHow the staff and board of management survey was run





The school staff and board of management survey was open to primary school staff and members of boards of management nationally. The target population was 84,285 staff and board members. A total of 32,999 responses were submitted, and 32,901 valid responses were kept after validation. That is a validated response rate of 39.0% of the eligible population. (Source: results summary report, section 4.1, p. 25.)

title: Primary School Survey 2026
section: There is a mismatch between the schools parents want for their children and the schools available to them
text:
There is a mismatch between the schools parents want for their children and the schools available to them


Figure 5. Stated ethos preference among households with a child not yet in school (n = 56,227), grouped by the type of school they intend to use. Each bar is 100% of the households intending that school type, split by whether they prefer a multi-denominational (green) or denominational (grey) ethos. This isolates demand for change: households intending a denominational school but preferring a multi-denominational one represent unmet demand, while households intending and preferring the same type represent confirmed preference. Percentages are recomputed from raw counts reported in the source, and the base (56,227) can’t be independently checked against the published survey spreadsheet. Source: Department of Education and Youth, Primary School Survey results summary report (June 2026), section 3.1.2, p. 14. Code: make_charts.py.
